styles.name: Flow
styles.description: Shows the direction of movement in a flowchart, connecting shapes to indicate the order in which steps, decisions, or events occur.

styles.name: Flow - Dashed
styles.description: Represents a secondary, optional, or informational flow. Something that isn't part of the main process but still relevant (like notes, annotations, or conditional relationships).

styles.name: Flow - Dotted
styles.description: Represents a weak, indirect, or reference-only connection, often used for comments, documentation links, or relationships that don't affect the actual process flow.

styles.name: Flow - Negative
styles.description: Indicates an exception or reverse path in the process. Typically represents an error, rejection, or unsuccessful outcome that sends the workflow to an alternate step.

styles.name: Flow - Positive
styles.description: Indicates the successful or desired path in a process showing that a step, condition, or decision led to a valid, approved, or completed outcome. It's the forward-moving branch that continues the main workflow.

styles.name: Invisible Edge
styles.description: Represents a hidden connection used only for layout control, not for actual process flow. It lets you align, route, or group elements cleanly without showing a visible line in the final diagram.

styles.name: Component
styles.description: Represents a distinct part of a system or process, typically a module, subsystem, or functional unit. It identifies a self‑contained element that performs a specific role within the larger workflow or architecture.

styles.name: Decision
styles.description: Represents a branch point where the process must choose between two or more paths based on a yes/no question, condition, or evaluation. It signals that the workflow will diverge depending on the outcome of that decision.

styles.name: Event
styles.description: Represents something that happens to the process, not an action performed, such as a start, trigger, interruption, or end. It marks a state change like a message arriving, a timer expiring, or a process completing.

styles.name: Extract
styles.description: Represents pulling information or material out of a larger source, often used to show that data, items, or inputs are being retrieved, separated, or filtered for use in the next step of the process.

styles.name: File
styles.description: Represents a document or record created, used, or stored during the process. It indicates that the step involves producing, referencing, or handling a physical or digital file.

styles.name: Folder
styles.description: Represents a collection of related files or documents, indicating that the process is accessing, storing, or organizing items within a grouped container. It signals that multiple documents or data elements are involved rather than a single file.

styles.name: Input
styles.description: Represents data or materials entering the process, showing that the workflow begins or continues by receiving information, resources, or user‑provided values. It marks the point where something is supplied to the system so the next step can proceed.

styles.name: Invisible Point
styles.description: A non-rendered connector marker used in diagrams to control how lines attach, route, or align without showing any visible symbol in the final flowchart.

styles.name: Manual Operation
styles.description: Represents a step performed by a person rather than a machine or system, indicating that human intervention is required to complete that part of the process.

styles.name: Merge
styles.description: Represents multiple incoming paths converging into a single flow, usually after different branches of a decision rejoin. It shows that the process continues along one unified path after alternative routes come together.

styles.name: Off Page Reference
styles.description: Shows that the flow continues somewhere else, usually on another page. It provides a labeled jump so the reader knows exactly where the process resumes.

styles.name: On Page Reference
styles.description: Shows that the flow continues somewhere else on the same page. It's a labeled connector used to avoid long or crossing lines while keeping the diagram tidy.

styles.name: Output
styles.description: Represents information or material leaving the process, showing that a step produces a result, report, display, or data that is sent onward or delivered to a user or system.

styles.name: Point
styles.description: Represents a specific position or marker in the flow, often used to show a connection, reference, or pivot within the process without performing an action itself.

styles.name: Predefined Process
styles.description: Represents a subroutine or established procedure that has already been created elsewhere. It signals that the flow should jump to a known, reusable process and then return to the main workflow once that routine is complete.

styles.name: Preparation
styles.description: Represents a setup or initialization step in a flowchart. It marks the point where the process gets ready for action, often used for tasks like initializing variables, setting conditions, or getting resources in place before the main workflow begins.

styles.name: Process
styles.description: Represents work being performed such as a task, action, or operation that moves the workflow forward.

styles.name: Stop
styles.description: Represents the completion or termination of the process. It marks the point where the workflow concludes and no further steps occur.

sql.sqlStatement: Examples showing how to see all the routes from a node, or all the routes leading to a node
Traditional query to pull in data and create a graph
SELECT [From Node] AS [ITEM], [To Node] AS [RELATED ITEM] FROM [Routes$]
PREVIEW
PUBLISH Use Case 1
This query specifies a START node. It will show all the branches which flow from that location.

SELECT 
  'SELECT [To Node], [From Node] AS [ITEM], [To Node] AS [RELATED ITEM]
     FROM [Routes$] WHERE [From Node] = ''{WHERE VALUE}''' 
              AS [TREE QUERY], 
  'A0'        AS [WHERE VALUE], 
  'To Node'   AS [WHERE COLUMN]
PREVIEW
PUBLISH Use Case 2
This query specifies a START node. It will show 3 levels of branches which flow from that location (root node + 3 ranks).

SELECT 
  'SELECT [To Node], [From Node] AS [ITEM], [To Node] AS [RELATED ITEM]
     FROM [Routes$] WHERE [From Node] = ''{WHERE VALUE}''' 
              AS [TREE QUERY], 
  'A0'        AS [WHERE VALUE], 
  'To Node'   AS [WHERE COLUMN],
  3           AS [MAX DEPTH]
PREVIEW
PUBLISH Use Case 3
This query specifies an END node. It will show all the branches which flow to that location.

SELECT 
  'SELECT [From Node], [From Node] AS [ITEM], [To Node] AS [RELATED ITEM]
     FROM [Routes$] WHERE [To Node] = ''{WHERE VALUE}''' 
              AS [TREE QUERY], 
  'A9'        AS [WHERE VALUE], 
  'From Node' AS [WHERE COLUMN]
PREVIEW
PUBLISH Use Case 4
This query specifies an END node. It will show up to 3 levels of branches which flow to that location. (3 ranks + final node)

SELECT 
  'SELECT [From Node], [From Node] AS [ITEM], [To Node] AS [RELATED ITEM]
     FROM [Routes$] WHERE [To Node] = ''{WHERE VALUE}''' 
              AS [TREE QUERY], 
  'A9'        AS [WHERE VALUE], 
  'From Node' AS [WHERE COLUMN],
  3           AS [MAX DEPTH]
PREVIEW
PUBLISH Use Case 5

Combine the examples to show the entire graph. Show 3 levels of routes leading to node A9 in blue, and 3 levels of routes
departing node A9 in red.
Step 1 - Get all the routes
SELECT [From Node] AS [ITEM], [To Node] AS [RELATED ITEM] FROM [Routes$]
Step 2 - Recurse 3 branches of nodes which converge on node A9. Change the edge color to blue

SELECT 
  'SELECT [From Node], [From Node] AS [ITEM], [To Node] AS [RELATED ITEM], ''color=blue'' as [Attributes]
     FROM [Routes$] WHERE [To Node] = ''{WHERE VALUE}''' 
              AS [TREE QUERY], 
  'A9'        AS [WHERE VALUE], 
  'From Node' AS [WHERE COLUMN],
  3           AS [MAX DEPTH]
Step 3 - Recurse 3 branches of nodes which branch out from node A9. Change the edge color to red

SELECT 
  'SELECT [To Node], [From Node] AS [ITEM], [To Node] AS [RELATED ITEM], ''color=red'' AS [Attributes]
     FROM [Routes$] WHERE [From Node] = ''{WHERE VALUE}''' 
              AS [TREE QUERY], 
  'A9'        AS [WHERE VALUE], 
  'To Node'   AS [WHERE COLUMN], 
  3           AS [MAX DEPTH]
PREVIEW
PUBLISH Use Case 6
Quick Help
Clear the 'data' worksheet
RESET
Specify the workbook containing the data
SET DATA FILE
Create the edges

SELECT [From Column] AS [Item], 
       [To Column]   AS [Related Item] 
FROM   [Worksheet Name$]
Create the nodes

SELECT [Node Id Column]    AS [Item],
       [Node Label Column] AS [Label],
       [Node Style Column] AS [Style Name]
FROM   [Worksheet Name$] 
WHERE  ...
Split text for labels at first blank after 10 characters

SELECT [Label Column] AS [Label],
       10             AS [SPLIT LENGTH],
       ...
Specify the line ending (\l, \n, \r, | etc.) to use when splitting a label

SELECT [Label Column] AS [Label],
       10             AS [SPLIT LENGTH],
       '\r'           AS [LINE ENDING],
       ...
Group nodes into a cluster

SELECT [Cluster Id Column]         AS [CLUSTER],
       [Cluster Label Column]      AS [CLUSTER LABEL],
       [Cluster Style Name Column] AS [CLUSTER STYLE NAME],
       [Cluster Attributes]        AS [CLUSTER ATTRIBUTES],
       [Cluster Tooltip Column]    AS [CLUSTER TOOLTIP],
       [Node Id Column]            AS [Item],
       [Node Label Column]         AS [Label],
       [Node Style Name Column]    AS [Style Name],
       ...
Group nodes into two level clusters

SELECT [Outer Cluster Id Column]         AS [CLUSTER],
       [Outer Cluster Label Column]      AS [CLUSTER LABEL],
       [Outer Cluster Style Name Column] AS [CLUSTER STYLE NAME],
       [Outer Cluster Attributes]        AS [CLUSTER ATTRIBUTES],
       [Outer Cluster Tooltip Column]    AS [CLUSTER TOOLTIP],

       [Inner Cluster Id Column]         AS [SUBCLUSTER],
       [Inner Cluster Label Column]      AS [SUBCLUSTER LABEL],
       [Inner Cluster Style Name Column] AS [SUBCLUSTER STYLE NAME],
       [Inner Cluster Attributes]        AS [SUBCLUSTER ATTRIBUTES],
       [Inner Cluster Tooltip Column]    AS [SUBCLUSTER TOOLTIP],

       [Node Id Column]                  AS [Item],
       [Node Label Column]               AS [Label],
       [Node Style Name Column]          AS [Style Name],
       ...

Loop count substitution strings (useful in sortv= attributes, style names, and labels). 
  %clc% = Cluster count
  %scc% = Subcluster count
  %rsc% = Record set count

SELECT 'sortv=%clc%'    AS [CLUSTER ATTRIBUTES],
       'Border %clc% '  AS [CLUSTER STYLE NAME],
       'sortv=%scc%'    AS [SUBCLUSTER ATTRIBUTES],
       'sortv=%rsc%'    AS [Attributes],
       ...
FROM   [Worksheet Name$] 
WHERE  ...
ORDER BY [Outer Cluster Label Column] ASC,
         [Inner Cluster Label Column] ASC,
         [Node Label Column]          ASC
Show the graph immediately after all SQL statements processed
PREVIEW [ AS ( DIRECTED | UNDIRECTED ) GRAPH ]
Publish graphs as files
PUBLISH [ ALL VIEWS ] [ AS ( DIRECTED | UNDIRECTED ) GRAPH ] [ file prefix ]
